Beriah
bĕ-rī´ăh
n. pr. m. (Hebrew Beri'ah, in trouble, or a gift)
The Chronicler supplies the etymology himself: Ephraim called his son Beriah because it went evil with his house, connecting the name with Hebrew ra'ah, evil or calamity.

Biblical Definition

Beriah is a name given out of grief and preserved as a tribe. The first bearer is a son of Asher: “And the sons of Asher; Jimnah, and Ishuah, and Isui, and Beriah, and Serah their sister: and the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel” (Gen 46:17). His descendants became a clan counted in the wilderness census: “Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the family of the Heberites: of Malchiel, the family of the Malchielites” (Num 26:45). The second bearer is the one whose naming Scripture explains. Ephraim's sons had been killed by the men of Gath, and the patriarch mourned many days; then: “And when he went in to his wife, she conceived, and bare a son, and he called his name Beriah, because it went evil with his house” (1Ch 7:23). A child born into a house still in mourning was named for the calamity that made room for him. Other Beriahs stand among the Benjamites (1Ch 8:13) and the Levites of David's courses (1Ch 23:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the Chronicler gives the sense, from the Hebrew for evil or calamity — because it went evil with his house.

expand to see more

BERIAH. A Hebrew proper name; explained in 1 Chronicles 7:23 from the word for evil or misfortune.

CALAMITY, n. Any great misfortune, or cause of misery; generally applied to events or disasters which produce extensive evils.

MOURN, v.i. To grieve; to lament; to sorrow; to be sorrowful.

Key Scripture

Gen 46:17 — "And the sons of Asher; Jimnah, and Ishuah, and Isui, and Beriah, and Serah their sister: and the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel."

Num 26:45 — "Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the family of the Heberites: of Malchiel, the family of the Malchielites."

1Ch 7:23 — "And when he went in to his wife, she conceived, and bare a son, and he called his name Beriah, because it went evil with his house."

1Ch 7:31 — "And the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel, who is the father of Birzavith."

Modern Corruption

Grief is expected to be resolved before life resumes, while Scripture records a father naming a son for the sorrow he was born into and the line continuing anyway.

expand to see more

1 Chronicles 7:23 is one of the quietest and hardest verses in the genealogies. Ephraim's sons were slain, he mourned many days, his brethren came to comfort him — and then he went in to his wife and she bare a son, and he named the boy for the disaster. The modern instinct would counsel against it: do not lay that on a child. Scripture does not comment. It reports the naming and moves on, and the line of Beriah runs forward into the tribe.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture allows grief to be named without requiring it to be resolved. Naomi called herself Mara and the book did not correct her. Ephraim called his son Beriah. Neither is presented as a model of faith or a failure of it; both are recorded, and in both cases God's purpose ran through the house that mourned. A daughter of this same Beriah, Sherah, went on to build three cities.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Beri'ah (H1283); the Chronicler links it to ra'ah (H7451), evil or calamity, in the phrase because it went evil with his house.

expand to see more

Hebrew Beri'ah (H1283) — Beriah; Genesis 46:17, 1 Chronicles 7:23, 8:13.

Hebrew ra'ah (H7451) — evil, calamity; the word the Chronicler uses to explain the name.

Hebrew 'abal (H56) — to mourn; Ephraim mourned many days.

Hebrew mishpachah (H4940) — family, clan; the Beriites of Numbers 26:44.

Hebrew 'Asher (H836) — Asher, happy; the tribe of the first Beriah, whose own name means blessed.

Usage

"“He called his name Beriah, because it went evil with his house” — the sorrow written into the child."

"“The family of the Beriites” — a clan out of a grief."

"The Chronicler explains the name and offers no consolation. The line continues."
